newsitem.title: UK: Asian currencies off lows in London, more pain seen.
newsitem.headline: Asian currencies off lows in London, more pain seen.

text.p: Southeast Asian currencies got a brief respite in London trade on Friday after tumbling to new lows in the Far East but foreign exchange dealers predicted more turmoil next week.

The renewed slide in Asian units, triggered by Indonesia's decision to move to a managed float system for the rupiah, saw increased trade in the exotic currencies in London after another hectic session in Singapore.
The Malaysian ringgit pulled back to 2.7800/7850 against the dollar by 1500 GMT after tumbling on the local market earlier to 2.8210.
There was talk of fund profit-taking in the currency, but dealers said they had seen no evidence of rumoured intervention from Bank Negara, the central bank.
The Singapore dollar was also off its lows, pulling back to 1.5150/1.5170 after earlier breaching 1.52 while the Indonesian rupiah was sitting under 2,900 after hitting 2,940.
But the Hong Kong dollar was fragile, hovering around the key support level of 7.75 to the dollar which dealers said could well fall on Monday, a holiday in Hong Kong.
"The market seems to be targeting the Hong Kong dollar as the last peg left in Asia," said one dealer at an Australian bank in London.
Mitul Kotecha, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank, said markets were likely to remain rocky.
"We'll probably see more pressure next week. Fundamentals have gone out of the window so it's very difficult to judge at what level the market is going to let these currencies stop," he said.
Gregory Cronie, a trader at Indover Bank in Amsterdam, reiterated the view that the economic fundamentals for the rupiah remained strong and did not justify current weakness.
But he said there were concerns that Indonesian corporates with foreign loans had been caught short of dollars following this week's currency plunge, adding further uncertainty to the market mix.
